A fixed reference point of known elevation used as the starting point for levelling work.
An imaginary line on a map joining points of equal elevation above a datum.
The process of determining differences in elevation between points on the earth's surface.
The first staff reading taken after setting up the level, on a point of known elevation.
The last staff reading taken before shifting the instrument, on a point whose elevation is to be found.
A precision instrument for measuring horizontal and vertical angles in traversing and triangulation.
An electronic instrument combining a theodolite with an EDM to measure angles and distances together.
The process of establishing intermediate points on a straight line between two survey stations.
A graphical method of surveying in which field work and plotting are done simultaneously.
Global Positioning System — satellite-based positioning used for locating survey points.
Plane: earth’s curvature neglected, small areas. Geodetic: curvature considered, large areas, precise far-apart points.
Map distance ÷ ground distance (unitless); e.g. 1 cm = 3 m → 1/300.
Graphical scale is drawn on the map and stays valid if paper shrinks; a numerical (RF) scale does not.
Work from whole to part; fix each new station by at least two measurements from fixed points.
Average step length found by pacing a known distance (usually 100 m); pacing error up to ±2% is acceptable.
20 m or 30 m; links of 20 cm; brass tags every 5 m, rings every metre.
100 ft, 100 links of 1 ft; tags every 10 links.
66 ft, 100 links of 0.66 ft (7.92 in); 10 chains = 1 furlong, 80 chains = 1 mile, 10 sq chains = 1 acre.
Arrows 30–40 cm (mark chain lengths); ranging rods 2–3 m, painted in alternate bands.
d = √(s² − h²); measure horizontally when slope exceeds 2%.
Simple triangulation: only sides measured, no angles; for small, fairly level, open areas.
Check line joins an apex to the opposite side to verify accuracy; tie line joins two points on main lines and picks up interior details.
Perpendicular distance from the chain line to an object; short ones by eye, long ones by cross staff or optical square.
Perpendicular BE bisected at D, perpendicular EF at E, F–D–C in line → BC = EF (BC = 3 EF if DE = BD/3).
Sides 9, 12, 15 m (or multiples) form a right angle; quick, ordinary field accuracy.
Four slotted arms on a 1.2–1.5 m staff; sets perpendiculars; moderate accuracy.
Horizon glass (half-silvered) + index glass (fully silvered); double reflection gives 90°; more accurate than a cross staff.
Angle between true and magnetic meridians; east or west.
BB = FB ± 180° (add if FB < 180°, subtract if FB > 180°).
Needle deflection by nearby iron, wires or ore; FB and BB do not differ by 180°; included angles unaffected.
Ring 0–360° clockwise, zero at the south end of the needle so readings are bearings from north.

Cumulative ∝ L (e.g. wrong chain length); compensating ∝ √L (random marking errors).
Graphical survey: field work and plotting done together; fast; low precision; good in magnetic areas.
Set up → centre (forked plumb bob) → level (spirit level, two directions) → orient (compass or back sighting).
45–60 cm straight edge with slit vane and hair vane; most used in farm surveys.
Rays from one station to all points; distances chained; small open areas.
Rays from two ends of a measured base; good for inaccessible points; intersection angles 30°–120°.
Set up at each station, back-sight the previous one, chain each leg; closing error visible on the sheet.

Apparent movement of cross hairs when the eye moves; remove by focusing eye-piece on hairs, then objective on staff.

Vertical distance between successive contours; usually 20–200 cm.
